canonical_title: Dr. Bloodmoney, or How We Got Along After the Bomb
author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: After nuclear catastrophe, scattered Northern California survivors rebuild an oddly humane world — haunted by a guilt-ridden physicist and a malevolent phocomelus with telekinetic power.
page_summary:
The bombs fall, and Dr. Bloodmoney follows a community of survivors around a devastated Bay Area as they improvise a new society: a repairman turned local leader, a floating disc jockey orbiting overhead in a stranded satellite, a girl with a talking twin lodged inside her body, and Hoppy Harrington, an armless-and-legless phocomelus whose telekinetic gifts curdle into a bid for power. Above it all hangs Bruno Bluthgeld, the physicist who believes himself responsible for the disaster.

Against the era's apocalyptic dread, PKD writes a post-nuclear world that is not a wasteland but a patched-together community — people getting along, as the subtitle promises, with resourcefulness and decency alongside the menace. Entropy and reconstruction run together: the world winds down and is rebuilt at once. The threat is less the radiation than the concentrated malevolence of a single damaged will.

Written around the time of the Cuban Missile Crisis and published in the mid-1960s, its title nods to Kubrick's Dr. Strangelove while turning the nuclear anxiety toward survival rather than annihilation.
